answer.rationale: Verify memory_c6 (multi-year incumbent commitment unlocked volume pricing without narrowing scope) and memory_c4 (benchmark-driven renegotiation recovered real margin on both price and payment terms). These two together inform the highest-leverage move: a renegotiation at the expiring 14-day primary contract. The 18% spend-cut mandate demands immediate unit-cost reduction, which memory_c6 suggests is achievable by extending the incumbent term in exchange for volume pricing. Memory_c4 confirms that competitive benchmarking at renewal has historically moved the incumbent on price and payment terms — exactly the levers finance needs. Crucially, memory_c1 (unverified but consistent with context) indicates that renewing with the incumbent preserved integration stability and caused zero delivery interruption, which directly protects the 94%-loaded assembly line that has no buffer. Switching primary vendor (memory_c2) could cut cost but introduces onboarding risk at the worst possible moment. Adding a second source (memory_c3) addresses resilience but does not hit the 18% target and would consume the single decision slot without solving the expiring contract. Deferring (memory_c5) is inapplicable here because the contract expires in 14 days with no auto-renew; month-to-month would lock in current pricing and forfeit the budget-cut target. Therefore: pull the archives for c6 and c4 to confirm the pricing and negotiation mechanisms, then commit to negotiate_terms with the incumbent — seek a multi-year extension at reduced unit cost, benchmarked against the low-cost alternative from memory_c2's experience as leverage — preserving the existing supply relationship and protecting the assembly line's committed volume.
